verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: about 99% of fission neutrons are prompt, emitted within about 10⁻¹⁴ s; the remaining fraction (about 0.65% for ²³⁵U) is emitted seconds later by excited fission fragments. That delay is what makes a reactor mechanically controllable. The book gives the definition alone; the reason is added here as the second mark.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Definition
steps.mark_note: Neutrons emitted after the fission, by the fragments
lines: Most fission neutrons appear at the instant of
Delayed neutrons are the few neutrons emitted
later, over a period of time, by the fission
steps.margin_note: First mark. "Liberated over a period of time after the fission" is the phrase.
steps.why: Some fission fragments are left with more neutrons than a stable nucleus can hold, and they release one seconds after the split rather than at the instant of the split.
common_mistakes: Saying delayed neutrons are slow neutrons. Slow refers to energy, delayed to time.

recall.must_convey: That delayed neutrons are the neutrons liberated over a period of time after the fission has taken place, from the fission fragments.
accept: emitted later by the fission fragments

steps.memory_tip: Delayed is about WHEN, thermal is about HOW FAST.

steps.label: Why they matter
steps.mark_note: The delay makes a reactor controllable
lines: They are less than one per cent of all fission
neutrons, but they arrive seconds after the
That delay is long enough for the control rods
to be moved, so a reactor can be controlled.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Link the delay to the movement of the control rods.
steps.why: Prompt neutrons alone appear within about 10⁻¹⁴ s, far too fast for any mechanical rod to follow. The small delayed fraction stretches the response time to seconds, which is what a reactor is regulated on.
common_mistakes: Saying delayed neutrons produce most of the energy. They are a very small fraction.
Leaving out the control rods. The delay matters because the rods can be moved in time.

recall.must_convey: That delayed neutrons are a very small fraction but arrive seconds later, which gives time for the control rods to act and makes a reactor controllable.

steps.memory_tip: A few seconds of delay is the whole margin a reactor is steered on.
